title: Affineness of finite-geometric-kernel homomorphisms over a Dedekind base
statement: Let $B$ be a Noetherian integrally closed domain of Krull dimension one and put $S=\operatorname{Spec}B$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Let $G\to S$ and $J\to S$ be separated flat group schemes of finite type [def-weil-flat-morphism, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Here a group scheme is a scheme over $S$ with multiplication, inverse and identity satisfying the group diagrams, and separated means that the diagonal is a closed immersion. Let $f:G\to J$ be an $S$-group homomorphism of finite type. For every algebraically closed field $k$ and ring map $B\to k$, assume that the scheme-theoretic kernel $\ker(f_k)=G_k\times_{J_k}\operatorname{Spec}k$, formed using the identity section of $J_k$, is finite over $k$ [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. Then $f$ is an affine morphism [pqf-def-affine-morphism]. Neither $G$ nor $J$ is assumed affine, smooth or connected, and no surjectivity or flatness of $f$ is assumed.

source.place: Proof of Proposition 6.3.16, printed p.229: finite geometric kernels imply quasi-finiteness, and a quasi-finite homomorphism between separated flat finite-type groups over a Dedekind base is affine. This statement combines those two consecutive assertions for an arbitrary homomorphism. Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states the Dedekind group-translation theorem.

proof.text: Fix $y\in J$ with nonempty scheme fibre $G_y$. Choose $x\in G_y$ and an algebraic closure $L$ of $\kappa(x)$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. The induced map $\kappa(y)\to L$ gives $y_L\in J_L(L)$ and a point $g\in(G_y)_L(L)$. On every $L$-scheme $T$, multiplication by $g_T$ sends $a\in\ker(f_L)(T)$ to $g_Ta\in f_L^{-1}(y_L)(T)$. Its inverse is $z\mapsto g_T^{-1}z$, since $f_L(g_T^{-1}z)=y_L^{-1}y_L=1$. These formulas are morphisms obtained by restricting multiplication and inverse, and their composites are identities by the group diagrams. Thus $(G_y)_L\simeq\ker(f_L)$ as $L$-schemes. The hypothesis applies to the composite $B\to\kappa(x)\to L$, so this kernel is finite over $L$.

source.place: Group identities; explicit fibre-translation construction supplying the finite-kernel-to-quasi-finite implication in Conrad Proposition 6.3.16, p.229.

proof.text: A finite scheme over $L$ has finitely many points by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-closed-map-finite-fibres]. The field extension $\kappa(y)\to L$ induces a surjective spectrum map by [lem-pc-field-extension-surjective]; its base change $(G_y)_L\to G_y$ is surjective by [lem-weil-pbc-surjective-base-change]. Hence $|G_y|$ is finite, being the image of a finite set. Empty fibres are already finite. All fibres of $f$ are therefore finite. Since $f$ is of finite type (including quasi-compactness) by hypothesis, [pqf-lem-qf-finitefibres] proves that $f$ is quasi-finite.

source.place: Tag 02NH finite-fibre criterion, with the explicit translation in step 1.

proof.text: The composite $G\xrightarrow fJ\to S$ is separated by hypothesis, so $f$ is separated by [lem-weil-pbc-separated-cancellation](b). Quasi-finiteness gives local quasi-finiteness by [pqf-lem-qf-locqf-qc], and finite type gives local finite type and quasi-compactness. Thus [lemma-nagata-quasi-affine-morphism-of-quasi-finite] applies with all four of its hypotheses and makes $f$ quasi-affine.

source.place: Separated quasi-finite Zariski-main quasi-affine factorization; existing DAG statement used in its full stated generality.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-relative-quasiaffine-group-envelope] to this $f$. Its base hypothesis holds since $B$ has dimension one, and the given $G,J$ are separated, flat and of finite type. Obtain the actual relative spectrum $H=\underline{\operatorname{Spec}}_J(f_*\mathcal O_G)$, homomorphisms $G\xrightarrow jH\xrightarrow qJ$, with $j$ a quasi-compact open immersion, $q$ affine and $qj=f$. Keep also its asserted isomorphism $\mathcal O_{H_K}\simeq(j_K)_*\mathcal O_{G_K}$ for $K=\operatorname{Frac}B$. In particular we have not inferred finite type for $H$.

source.place: Tag 01SM canonical envelope, with the separately stated relative group construction.

proof.text: For each $s\in S$, base change preserves the group diagrams, and [lem-weil-pbc-open-immersion-base-change] preserves the open immersion, so $j_s:G_s\to H_s$ is a group homomorphism with open point image. By [lem-sfb-field-open-group-image-closed] over $\kappa(s)$, its image is closed. Apply this also at the generic point: $j_K(G_K)$ is open and closed in $H_K$. Its complement must be empty, because on that open complement the isomorphism $\mathcal O_{H_K}\simeq(j_K)_*\mathcal O_{G_K}$ of [lem-sfb-relative-quasiaffine-group-envelope] would identify the structure sheaf with the zero sheaf. At a point of a nonempty scheme the local ring is nonzero. Thus $j_K$ has full image; as an open immersion it identifies $G_K$ with $H_K$.

source.place: Tag 047S over each residue field, followed by generic saturation using the canonical function comparison.

proof.text: View $j$ as the inclusion of its image open $U\subseteq H$. It is quasi-compact, it contains the whole generic fibre by step 5, and $U_s$ is closed in $H_s$ for every $s$ by that same step. Therefore [lem-sfb-dedekind-vertical-clopen-open-affine] applied to $X=H$ makes $j$ affine. This criterion imposes no finite-type hypothesis on $H$. Finally $q$ is affine by step 4, so [lem-weil-pbc-affine-composition] proves that $f=qj$ is affine.

source.place: Tag 07ZT principal-boundary argument, then composition of affine morphisms.
